front.title: Consent Receipt Binding for Task-Scoped Authorization

abstract.t: This document defines a signed consent receipt for task-scoped authorization between local agents. A receipt records a user's decision to allow or deny a described action, binds that decision to a task, an agent, an audience, an action set, and a resource set, and can be verified offline. The document also defines the consent request, the reservation ordering that avoids a circular dependency between a receipt and a capability token, the audit events that accompany consent and side effects, and an informative mapping to ISO/IEC 27560. It does not define a user interface, a transport, or a capability token format.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Local agents can perform actions that leave the device, change shared state, or are difficult to reverse. A user needs a way to approve such an action for a specific task, with a clear description of who is acting, what will happen, which data will be used, and how long the approval lasts. The approval must be verifiable by an agent that did not observe the user interface, and it must not silently become a general permission for the agent.

This document defines a consent receipt for that purpose. A Policy and Consent Service (PCS) constructs a consent request from a capability descriptor and from policy. The user, or an operating-system consent surface acting for the user, grants or denies the request. A grant produces a signed receipt. The receipt is bound to the task, the agent, the audience, the requested actions and resources, the risk class, and a validity window. A Capability Authority (CA) verifies the receipt before issuing the capability token that the agent will present to its audience.

The receipt is not a general-purpose access token. It is an authorization artifact for one task-scoped decision. It can be audited, exported, and redacted, but it cannot be reused for another task or another audience.

section.name: Scope
section.t: This document defines:

ul.li: the structure of a consent request and its intent preview;
the structure of a consent receipt;
the signature and canonicalization rules for a receipt;
the ordering that lets a receipt reference a capability identifier before the capability is active;
the binding rules between a receipt and a capability token;
the audit events for consent, effects, and revocation; and
an informative mapping to ISO/IEC 27560.

section.t: This document does not define a user-interface layout, a transport binding, a capability token format, a discovery protocol, or an audit storage engine. The capability token format is defined in a companion document.

section.name: Relation to Other Work
section.t: ISO/IEC 27560 specifies a consent record information structure. It is useful for interoperability with privacy-management systems, but it is not an authorization protocol for local agents. This document defines a task-scoped authorization receipt and provides an informative mapping to the ISO structure in .

The Kantara Initiative's consent receipt work provides a human-readable and machine-readable record of a consent decision. This document shares the goal of a verifiable record but adds the binding to a local task, audience, capability identifier, and audit chain that multi-agent execution requires.

OAuth 2.0 Rich Authorization Requests describes structured authorization details. A consent receipt can be carried as an authorization detail in an OAuth deployment, but this document does not define an OAuth grant type.

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
This document uses the following terms:

dl.dd: An addressable software component that requests or performs an action. An agent is identified by an agent URI.
The agent that will perform the approved action.
The component that issues and revokes capability tokens. It verifies a consent receipt before activating a token that needs one.
The component that evaluates policy, computes the effective risk class, constructs consent requests, and records the user's decision.
A structured description of the action for which consent is sought.
A signed record of a grant or denial for one consent request.
An allocated but inactive capability identifier. A receipt can reference a reservation before the capability is issued.
A unit of work with an identifier, a root, and an optional parent. A receipt is bound to exactly one task.
One of L0 through L4. L3 and L4 actions require a receipt.

section.name: Risk Classes

tr.td: Send a message or submit a form
Per use, with batch or time limits

section.t: The capability descriptor declares a risk class. The PCS computes the effective class from the descriptor, the data labels, the target, and the context. The PCS MAY raise the class but MUST NOT lower it. A consent request MUST carry the effective class that the PCS used.

section.name: Task Scope
section.t: Every receipt is bound to one task identifier. A task-level grant may cover multiple uses within that task, but it MUST NOT extend to a sibling task, a child task, or a later task by implication. A child task that needs an L3 or L4 action needs a receipt whose task_id is the child task, or a receipt whose scope explicitly covers the child task and whose audience matches the child's audience.
A batch grant MUST state its action set, resource set, task scope, and time window. A user interface that offers "allow for this task" MUST show the resulting scope before the decision is recorded.

section.name: Consent Fatigue
section.t: Asking for every low-risk action causes users to approve without reading. This document therefore separates the default treatment by risk class, as shown in . L3 actions may use a bounded task-level grant, and L4 actions require a strong confirmation. A deployment SHOULD measure how often users deny or revoke grants; a high denial rate is evidence that the request text or the scope is not useful.

section.name: Consent Request
section.t: A consent request is a message from the PCS to the user or to the operating-system consent surface. It describes one decision. The request is not itself an authorization; only a grant receipt is.

tr.td: An opaque identifier for this request. It is distinct from the message identifier and is used by the decision.
The task to which the decision will be bound.
The agent that will exercise the resulting capability.
The agent that will perform the action.
The action set for which consent is sought.
The resource set for which consent is sought.
The effective risk class computed by the PCS.
A short human-readable description of the action.
The offered decisions. This document defines allow_once, allow_task, and deny.
An RFC 3339 timestamp after which the request is no longer actionable.
The request timestamp in RFC 3339 format .

section.name: Intent Preview
section.t: The intent preview makes the decision concrete. It contains:

dl.dd: A human-readable name of the agent that will act.
A one-sentence description of the action.
An array of data categories or opaque references that will be used. It SHOULD NOT contain raw personal data.
An object with optional money and external_calls members.
An ISO 8601 duration describing the proposed validity.
A boolean indicating whether the action cannot be undone.

section.t: The PCS MUST derive the preview from the capability descriptor and from policy, not only from text supplied by the requesting agent. If the agent supplies a summary, the PCS MUST treat it as untrusted input.

section.name: Options
section.t: The options array tells the consent surface which decisions it may return:

ul.li: allow_once grants a single use. The resulting receipt MUST have max_uses equal to one.
allow_task grants a bounded number of uses within the task. The receipt MUST carry a positive max_uses and an expiry.
deny records a refusal. A denial is terminal for the request.

section.t: A consent surface MUST NOT return an option that the request did not offer.

section.name: Example Request
section.sourcecode: { "osap": "0.1", "type": "consent.request", "id": "msg_03", "from": "agent://system/policy#0", "to": { "user": "user://local/example-user" }, "body": { "schema": "osap.consent.request/v1", "data": { "request_id": "creq_01J8Z3K4M5N6P7Q8R9S0T1V2W3", "task_id": "task_01J8Z3K4M5N6P7Q8R9S0T1V2W3", "agent": "agent://com.example.orchestrator/main#1a2b", "audience": "agent://com.example.messaging/agent#4d", "actions": ["messaging.send"], "resources": ["contact://directory/example-contact"], "risk": "L3", "summary": "Send one meeting summary message", "intent_preview": { "actor": "Orchestrator Agent", "what": "Send 1 message", "data": [ "meeting summary (reference)", "contact: example contact" ], "cost": { "money": 0, "external_calls": 1 }, "ttl": "PT10M", "irreversible": false }, "options": ["allow_once", "allow_task", "deny"], "expires_at": "2026-11-10T10:24:45Z" } }, "ts": "2026-11-10T10:14:45Z" }

section.name: Grant
section.t: A grant decision produces a receipt and, when the request is part of a capability issuance, the identifiers needed to activate the capability. The grant response MUST contain:

ul.li: receipt_id: the identifier of the signed receipt;
cap_id: the reserved capability identifier that the receipt authorizes;
expires_at: the receipt expiry; and
constraints: the effective constraints, including max_uses.

section.t: The receipt MUST bind the user, the agent, the task, the action set, the resource set, the audience, the risk class, and the validity window. A grant for allow_once MUST set max_uses to one. A grant MUST NOT have an expiry later than the request's expires_at when that member is present.

section.name: Deny
section.t: A denial MUST produce a structured response with a reason code and, when available, one or more alternatives. A denial is terminal for the request. A denied request MUST NOT be silently retried with a broader scope. A new request requires a new identifier and, when the policy requires it, a new user decision.

section.name: Reservation Protocol
section.t: A capability token that needs a receipt must carry consent_receipt_id, and a receipt must reference the cap_id that it authorizes. This creates a circular dependency. The following order breaks it:

ol.li: The receiver, through the PCS, evaluates the action and decides that consent is required.
The CA reserves a cap_id. A reservation allocates an identifier but does not sign a token and does not make the capability usable.
The user or operating-system consent surface issues a receipt that references the reserved cap_id and the target audience.
The CA verifies the receipt, issues the capability token with consent_receipt_id set, and activates the token.
If the request is denied, expires, or is revoked before activation, the reserved cap_id MUST NOT become usable.

section.t: An unactivated reservation MUST NOT pass any routing or authorization check. A reservation SHOULD expire on the same schedule as its consent request.

section.name: Revocation
section.t: Revoking a receipt MUST invalidate every capability token that references it, including descendants that inherited the receipt. A revocation MUST be recorded in the audit log and communicated to affected agents. Revocation is terminal for that receipt: a later decision requires a new request and a new receipt.
A receiver MUST check receipt status before executing an L3 or L4 action. If the receiver cannot check status, it MUST deny the action.

tr.td: Receipt format version. The value is 0.1.
An opaque, globally unique identifier for this receipt.
The user principal that made the decision.
The agent that will exercise the resulting capability.
The task to which the decision is bound.
The reserved or issued capability identifier that this receipt authorizes.
The agent that will perform the action.
The effective risk class for the decision.
An object with max_uses and expires_at. It MUST be present for a grant.
An opaque digest of the policy or notice that the user saw. It lets an auditor check that the decision was made against a known policy without embedding the policy text.
The decision time in RFC 3339 format.
A namespaced extension object. It participates in the signed bytes.

section.name: Example Receipt
section.t: The signature value and the policy hash in this example are illustrative and are not valid values.

section.name: Canonicalization and Proof
section.t: A receipt is serialized as UTF-8 JSON. The signature covers the canonical byte sequence of the receipt with the proof member removed. The canonicalization rules are the same as for a capability token:

ol.li: the value is a JSON object;
members are sorted by the Unicode code point order of their names;
strings use the shortest RFC 8259 escape, with non-ASCII characters emitted as UTF-8; and
all numbers are integers; floating-point numbers are rejected.

section.t: These rules are a profile of the JSON Canonicalization Scheme that is deterministic for receipts because the format restricts numeric values to integers. A parser MUST reject duplicate member names. A verifier MUST NOT accept a receipt whose signature was computed over a different serialization.
The proof object has three members:

dl.dd: The value EdDSA, using Ed25519 as defined in RFC 8032 .
The identifier of the user or operating-system key that signed the receipt.
The signature encoded with base64url as defined in Section 5 of RFC 4648 , without padding.

section.t: A receipt MUST be signed by the user or by an operating-system consent service acting for the user. An agent MUST NOT sign its own receipt. A verifier MUST resolve kid through a trusted key registry and MUST reject an unknown, revoked, or expired key.

section.name: Validation Order
section.t: A verifier SHOULD process a receipt in the following order:

ol.li: check the syntax, version, and required members;
resolve proof.kid and verify the signature;
check constraints.expires_at against the current time;
check the binding to the request: user, agent, task_id, audience, actions, and resources; and
check that max_uses has not been exhausted.

section.t: A denial receipt is not an authorization. A verifier that expects an authorization MUST reject a receipt whose decision is deny.

section.name: Expiry and Scope
section.t: A receipt MUST have an expiry. An expired receipt MUST NOT be used, even if the associated capability token has not expired. A receipt's action and resource sets MUST exactly cover the request; a prefix match, a case-insensitive match, or an implicit wildcard is not sufficient. If a capability needs a narrower scope than the receipt, the CA MAY issue a narrower token, but it MUST NOT issue a broader one.
A task-level grant SHOULD have a short validity window and a finite max_uses. A receipt with no finite use count is not defined by this document.

section.name: Offline Verification
section.t: A receipt is designed to be verifiable offline: the verifier needs the receipt, the public key identified by kid, and the canonicalization rules. Offline verification proves that the user or consent service signed the stated decision. It does not prove that the receipt has not been revoked since the verifier last fetched status. A verifier that requires freshness MUST obtain a current status or rely on a short expiry.

section.name: Binding to Capability Tokens
section.t: A capability token that requires consent MUST carry consent_receipt_id. The receipt and the token MUST agree on task_id, audience, actions, and resources. The receipt's agent MUST equal the token's subject. The receipt's user MUST be the principal on whose behalf the token is issued.

If the token's scope is a subset of the receipt's scope, the token is valid. If the token asks for an action or resource that the receipt does not cover, the CA MUST reject the issuance with POLICY_CONSENT_SCOPE_MISMATCH. If the receipt is expired or revoked, the token MUST be treated as unusable and the receiver MUST reject it with POLICY_CONSENT_EXPIRED.

A child token may reference the same receipt only when the receipt still covers the child's task, audience, actions, and resources. A delegation to a new audience normally requires a new receipt because the original receipt's audience does not match the child's audience.

section.name: Event Shape
section.t: Every audit event contains at least the following members:

tr.td: The identifier of the user intent that caused the event.
The task associated with the event.
The session associated with the event.
The agent or service that produced the event.
The event type, such as consent.granted or effect.executed.
intent or outcome for effect.* events; absent for every other event.
The target of the action, expressed as a resource identifier.
allow, deny, or another deployment-defined decision.
The policy or notice reference used for the decision.
The receipt that authorized the action, when one applies.
Opaque references to context handles or objects used.
The event time in RFC 3339 format.
The hash of the previous event in the same trace.

section.name: Required Event Types
section.t: An implementation that records the consent and effect lifecycle MUST use the following event types:

ul.li: agent.registered and agent.registration_denied;
capability.issued, capability.attenuated, capability.attenuation_denied, capability.exercised, and capability.revoked;
discovery.query and discovery.result;
message.sent and message.delivered;
context.resolve and context.denied;
consent.requested, consent.granted, and consent.denied;
effect.intent, effect.executed, and effect.reconciled;
egress.blocked; and
error.

section.name: Two-Phase Effects
section.t: An L3 or L4 side effect uses two audit records. Before the side effect, the implementation writes effect.intent with phase equal to intent, including the target, a digest of the parameters, the consent receipt, and an idempotency key. After the side effect, it writes effect.executed with phase equal to outcome and a reference to the intent record.

If a restart finds an intent with no outcome, the effect state is unknown. The implementation MUST require reconciliation before replaying the action. Reconciliation records an outcome of executed or not_executed; it does not re-execute the side effect.

section.name: Hash Chain
section.t: Each event's hash is computed over the canonical event body with the hash member removed. The body includes prev_hash. The first event in a trace uses a fixed genesis value. A verifier recomputes the hash chain and checks that every prev_hash matches the previous event's hash. A mismatch, a missing event, or a duplicate audit_id is an integrity failure.
The hash chain proves that the recorded sequence was not modified without detection. It does not prove that every real-world action was recorded, and it does not make an audit record confidential.

section.name: Trace and Redaction
section.t: A user intent has one trace_id. Every agent hop records a causation identifier, so a user can view the cross-application chain. An export MUST preserve hash and prev_hash. Sensitive fields MAY be replaced by a commitment using a salt that is unique to the export. A verifier of a redacted export can check the chain and the commitments, but cannot recover the clear text. A verifier MUST be told that the export is redacted and MUST NOT treat it as a full record.

section.name: Informative Mapping to ISO/IEC 27560
section.t: ISO/IEC 27560 specifies a consent record information structure. The following table maps the receipt members in this document to the concepts in that structure. The mapping is informative. It does not claim that a receipt alone is an ISO-conformant consent record, because a complete record also needs notice, controller, purpose, and jurisdiction information that a local authorization artifact may not carry.

tr.td: Recipient or processor acting for the principal
Reference to the notice or policy
Task scope, as an extension for local authorization

section.t: An implementation that exports a receipt into a 27560-compatible record SHOULD keep the original receipt identifier and signature so that the exported record can be traced back to the authorization decision.

section.name: Forged Receipts
section.t: An agent might try to create its own receipt. A verifier MUST require a signature by a key that is trusted for the user or for the operating-system consent service. A receipt signed by the requesting agent's key MUST be rejected, even if the agent is otherwise trusted for the action.

section.name: Consent Phishing and Misleading Requests
section.t: A malicious agent can describe an action inaccurately. The PCS MUST derive the preview from the capability descriptor and from policy, and the consent surface MUST display the effective action, resource, risk, cost, and duration. The user's decision applies to the scope shown in the receipt, not to the agent's prose. A mismatch between the preview and the receipt scope is a security failure.

section.name: Replay
section.t: A receipt is bound to a task, an audience, an action set, a resource set, and a capability identifier. Reusing it for another task or audience fails the binding check. A receipt with a finite max_uses must be counted atomically, or the use count can be exceeded by concurrent requests.

section.name: Reservation and Activation Race
section.t: The reservation protocol separates allocation from activation. An attacker that learns a reserved cap_id must not be able to activate it without a valid receipt. Activation MUST verify the receipt's signature, decision, expiry, and scope before changing the reservation to active. A denied, expired, or revoked reservation MUST remain unusable.

section.name: Audit Integrity
section.t: The hash chain detects modification of recorded events but not omission of events that were never written. An implementation that requires an audit record before an L3 or L4 side effect must make the write durable before the effect. A redacted export proves integrity and commitment consistency, not the original content.

section.name: Revocation
section.t: A revoked receipt must invalidate every capability that references it. A receiver that cannot check receipt status must deny an L3 or L4 action. Cached status must have a bounded freshness interval. A revocation notification is advisory; it is not a substitute for the execution-time status check.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Consent receipts contain a user identifier, an agent identifier, a task identifier, and resource identifiers. They should carry the minimum information needed to prove the decision. Resource identifiers should be opaque handles rather than paths or personal data. The policy_hash should commit to the notice the user saw without embedding the notice text.

Audit exports should support redaction with per-export salts. Retention should be limited to the period needed for user review, dispute resolution, and legal obligations. A task identifier should not become a stable cross-application tracking identifier.
When a receipt is exported into an ISO/IEC 27560 record, the exporter should apply the same data-minimization rules and should not add personal data that the local authorization did not need.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions.
